item.title: AWS Backup: Schedule and Protect Your Data Across AWS Services
item.description: KMS protects your data from being read. AWS Backup protects it from being lost. It is one place to schedule, run and keep backups for many AWS services…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
KMS protects your data from being read. AWS Backup protects it from being lost. It is one place to schedule, run and keep backups for many AWS services, instead of setting up each service on its own.

What AWS Backup does

  • It gives you a central place to manage backups across services such as EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS and S3.
  • You describe what you want in a backup plan, and AWS Backup runs it on a schedule.
  • Backups are stored in a backup vault, which can be encrypted with a KMS key.
  • Every backup job is tracked, so you can see what ran and what failed.

Key concepts

Piece What it is
Backup plan The rules: schedule, lifecycle and which vault to use
Backup rule One schedule inside a plan, such as daily at 05:00 UTC
Resource assignment Which resources the plan covers, by ID or by tag
Backup vault The container that stores recovery points
Recovery point One saved backup that you can restore from
Lifecycle When a backup moves to cold storage or expires

Good to know

  • Assign resources by tag, for example Backup = daily, so new resources are picked up automatically.
  • Set a retention period so old backups do not pile up and cost money.
  • A restore creates a new resource from the recovery point. It does not overwrite the old one.
  • Vault Lock can stop backups from being deleted too early.
  • Cross-Region and cross-account copies help with disaster recovery.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open AWS Backup in the console and choose Create backup plan.
  2. Pick Build a new plan and name it demo-daily.
  3. Add a rule: Daily, with retention of 7 days (keep it short to limit cost).
  4. Use the Default backup vault.
  5. Create the plan, then choose Assign resources.
  6. Select Include specific resource types, pick one small resource such as an EBS volume, or assign by tag Backup = daily.
  7. Choose On-demand backup for the same resource to test it now, and wait for the job to finish under Jobs.
  8. Open the recovery point and look at the Restore option.
  9. Clean up: delete the recovery point, the resource assignment and the backup plan.

Common mistakes

  • Making a backup plan but forgetting to assign resources, so nothing is backed up.
  • Never testing a restore. A backup you cannot restore is not a backup.
  • Keeping backups forever and paying for storage you do not need.
  • Keeping backups only in one Region and one account.
  • Forgetting that a backup vault key in KMS must stay available.

Key takeaways

  • AWS Backup gives one place to schedule and track backups across services.
  • A plan holds the rules, a vault holds the recovery points.
  • Assign resources by tag so new ones are covered.
  • Test a restore, and set retention to control cost.

Tomorrow I'll recap the AWS security and operations topics from this series.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Subflows Cheat Sheet: Reusing Logic Across Flows and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Flows can get big fast. A subflow lets you build a piece of logic once and call it from other flows. Admin II interviews ask about it often. A flow that…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Flows can get big fast. A subflow lets you build a piece of logic once and call it from other flows. Admin II interviews ask about it often.

Subflows at a Glance

Piece What it does Key point
Subflow element Calls another flow from a flow The called flow must be active
Input variable Sends a value into the subflow Tick Available for input
Output variable Sends a value back Tick Available for output
Flow type Which flows can be called Autolaunched flows and Screen Flows can be subflows

Interview Q&A

1. What is a subflow?

A flow that another flow calls with the Subflow element. The parent flow pauses at that element, the subflow runs, and then the parent carries on.

Tip: Think of it like a function you can reuse.

2. Why use one?

To reuse the same logic in many flows, to keep a big flow readable, and to change the logic in one place.

Tip: Name subflows clearly, for example Sub - Create Follow-Up Task.

3. How do you pass values in and out?

Create variables in the subflow and tick Available for input or Available for output. In the Subflow element you then set each input and can store each output.

Tip: Pass only what the subflow needs.

4. Which flows can you call?

Autolaunched flows and Screen Flows. The flow you call must be active.

Tip: Keep a version active before you call it from a parent.

5. How do errors behave?

If the subflow fails, the error comes back to the parent. Add a fault path on the Subflow element, so the parent can show a message or roll back.

Tip: Fault paths work on the Subflow element too.

6. Do subflows share limits with the parent?

Yes. A subflow that runs in the same transaction uses the same governor limits as the parent flow.

Tip: Do not hide a Get Records inside a loop by putting it in a subflow.

Scenario Question

"Three flows all create a follow-up Task in the same way. How do you stop copying the same elements?"

  1. Build one Autolaunched Flow that creates the Task
  2. Add input variables for Subject and Related Id
  3. Activate it
  4. In each parent flow, add a Subflow element and set the inputs
  5. Add a fault path on the Subflow element

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create an Autolaunched Flow named Sub - Create Follow-Up Task.
  2. Add a text variable TaskSubject and tick Available for input.
  3. Add a text variable RelatedId and tick Available for input.
  4. Add Create Records for Task with Subject = {!TaskSubject} and WhatId = {!RelatedId}.
  5. Save and Activate it.
  6. Open your Screen Flow from this series and add a Subflow element.
  7. Pick Sub - Create Follow-Up Task and set the two inputs.
  8. Add a fault path to the Subflow element, then Debug and check the new Task.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Subflow element = call another flow
  • Called flow = must be active
  • Input / Output = Available for input / output
  • Fault path = add it on the Subflow element
  • Limits = shared with the parent in the same transaction

Key Takeaways

  • Build repeated logic once and call it as a subflow.
  • Give subflows clear names and pass only what they need.
  • Activate the subflow before you call it.
  • Add a fault path on the Subflow element.

Next up: a quick recap of the Flow series so far, and what to practice for the exam.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Do you reuse flows with subflows? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS KMS: How Encryption Keys Protect Your Data in AWS
item.description: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store both lean on one thing underneath: AWS KMS, the Key Management Service. KMS creates and controls the encryption keys…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Secrets Manager and Parameter Store both lean on one thing underneath: AWS KMS, the Key Management Service. KMS creates and controls the encryption keys that many AWS services use to protect your data.

What KMS does

  • It creates and manages KMS keys, and these keys never leave the service in plain form.
  • Other services, such as S3, EBS and Secrets Manager, call KMS to encrypt and decrypt data for you.
  • Every use of a key can be controlled with permissions and recorded in CloudTrail.
  • Keys are Regional. A key lives in the Region where you create it.

Types of keys

Type Who manages it Notes
AWS owned key AWS Used by some services behind the scenes, and you do not see it
AWS managed key AWS, in your account Named like aws/s3, rotated automatically, and you cannot change its policy
Customer managed key You You control the key policy, aliases, rotation and deletion

Key concepts

  • Key policy: the main access control for a key. IAM policies can only grant access if the key policy allows it.
  • Alias: a friendly name such as alias/demo-key, which points to a key.
  • Symmetric key: one key for both encrypt and decrypt. It is the default type.
  • Envelope encryption: KMS encrypts a small data key, and the data key encrypts the large data. The direct Encrypt call is limited to 4 KB.
  • Key rotation: for customer managed keys you can turn on automatic rotation.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Create a key: aws kms create-key --description "demo key" and note the KeyId.
  2. Add an alias: aws kms create-alias --alias-name alias/demo-key --target-key-id <KeyId>
  3. Make a file: echo "hello kms" > hello.txt
  4. Encrypt it: aws kms encrypt --key-id alias/demo-key --plaintext fileb://hello.txt --query CiphertextBlob --output text | base64 --decode > hello.enc
  5. Decrypt it: aws kms decrypt --ciphertext-blob fileb://hello.enc --query Plaintext --output text | base64 --decode
  6. Turn on rotation: aws kms enable-key-rotation --key-id <KeyId>
  7. In the console, open the key and read its key policy.
  8. Clean up: aws kms delete-alias --alias-name alias/demo-key, then aws kms schedule-key-deletion --key-id <KeyId> --pending-window-in-days 7

Common mistakes

  • Scheduling a key for deletion while data still depends on it. Once the key is gone, that data cannot be decrypted.
  • Using a broad permission such as kms:* when a role only needs to encrypt and decrypt.
  • Forgetting that the key policy must allow access, even when the IAM policy does.
  • Trying to encrypt large files directly instead of using envelope encryption.
  • Leaving practice keys behind. A customer managed key is billed per month, plus requests.

Key takeaways

  • KMS creates and controls the keys that protect your data across AWS.
  • The key policy decides who can use a key, so write it carefully.
  • Use customer managed keys when you need control over policy, rotation and deletion.
  • Plan before you delete a key, and clean up practice keys.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS Backup and how to protect your data with scheduled backups.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Delete and Roll Back Records Cheat Sheet: Removing Data Safely and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: After Get, Create and Update comes the last of the data elements: Delete Records. It pairs with Roll Back Records, which undoes saves when something goes…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
After Get, Create and Update comes the last of the data elements: Delete Records. It pairs with Roll Back Records, which undoes saves when something goes wrong. Admin II interviews love this pair.

Delete and Roll Back at a Glance

Element What it does Key point
Delete Records Deletes records By conditions, or by a record or collection
Roll Back Records Undoes pending record changes in the transaction Used on a fault path after a failed save
Fault path Where the flow goes when an element fails Add it to elements that save or delete
Transaction A group of changes saved together A screen or Pause ends it

Interview Q&A

1. How does Delete Records find the records?

Two ways: specify conditions and delete every record that matches, or use the Ids stored in a record variable or collection.

Tip: With conditions, test the filter first. A loose filter deletes more than you expect.

2. Where do deleted records go?

Deleted records can usually be restored from the Recycle Bin for a limited time. Deleting a parent record can also affect its child records, depending on the relationship.

Tip: Check the relationship type before you delete a parent.

3. Should you delete inside a loop?

No. Collect the records in a collection variable with an Assignment, then use one Delete Records after the loop.

Tip: The same rule applies to Create and Update.

4. What does Roll Back Records do?

It reverses the record changes made earlier in the current transaction, so the data goes back to how it was before those changes.

Tip: It undoes record changes only, so plan what else the flow has already done.

5. When do you use it?

When the flow does several saves in a row and a later one fails. Put Roll Back Records on the fault path so a half-finished set of changes does not stay in the org.

Tip: Then show the user a clear message with {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.

6. What is a transaction in a flow?

The group of changes that are saved together. In a Screen Flow, changes are saved when the flow reaches a screen or a Pause, so rolling back only reaches back to that point.

Tip: Put related saves together, with no screen between them.

Scenario Question

"The flow creates a follow-up Task and then updates the Opportunity. If the update fails, the Task must not stay behind."

  1. Create Records for the Task, then Update Records for the Opportunity, with no screen between them
  2. Add a fault path to the Update Records element
  3. On the fault path, add Roll Back Records
  4. Then show a screen with {!$Flow.FaultMessage}

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open your Screen Flow from this series with the Create Records (Task) and Update Records (Opportunity) elements.
  2. Make sure there is no screen between the Create and the Update.
  3. On the fault path of Update Records, add a Roll Back Records element named Undo Changes.
  4. After it, add a screen that shows {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.
  5. To test, add a validation rule on Opportunity that always fails for your test record, or temporarily set a required field to blank, then Debug the flow.
  6. Check that no new Task was left behind, then remove your test rule.
  7. Optional: add Delete Records on Task with the condition Id equals {!NewTaskId} to remove a test Task you created.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Delete Records = by conditions, or by record or collection
  • Recycle Bin can restore deleted records for a limited time
  • Never delete inside a loop
  • Roll Back Records = undo record changes in this transaction
  • Use it on a fault path
  • A screen or Pause ends the transaction

Key Takeaways

  • Test the conditions before you delete records.
  • Collect records in a collection, then delete once after the loop.
  • Roll Back Records keeps a failed multi-step save from leaving partial data.
  • Keep related saves together, with no screen between them.

Next up: subflows, and how to call one flow from another.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Do you use Roll Back Records? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store: Keep Secrets Out of Your Code
item.description: Systems Manager gave me a way into instances without SSH. The next question is where an application should keep its database password and settings so they…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Systems Manager gave me a way into instances without SSH. The next question is where an application should keep its database password and settings so they never end up in code. AWS has two good answers: Secrets Manager and Parameter Store.

The two services

  • AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets such as database credentials and API keys, encrypts them with AWS KMS, and can rotate them automatically.
  • Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration values and secrets in a path-style hierarchy, such as /myapp/prod/db-host.
  • Both are accessed with an API call and controlled with IAM permissions.

How they compare

Secrets Manager Parameter Store
Best for Credentials that need rotation App settings and simple secrets
Rotation Built in, using Lambda Not built in
Encryption Always, with KMS Only for the SecureString type
Cost Billed per secret per month, plus API calls Standard parameters are free; Advanced parameters cost extra
Size Larger values Standard parameters are up to 4 KB

Check the current pricing page before you rely on these numbers.

Parameter types

  • String for plain text such as a hostname
  • StringList for comma-separated values
  • SecureString for values encrypted with KMS

Access with IAM

  • The caller needs permission such as secretsmanager:GetSecretValue or ssm:GetParameter.
  • For encrypted values it also needs permission to use the KMS key, such as kms:Decrypt.
  • Give an application role only the paths or secrets it needs.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

Use a fake value only. Never put a real password in a practice exercise.

  1. Store a plain parameter: aws ssm put-parameter --name /demo/app/db-host --value mydb.example.internal --type String
  2. Store an encrypted one: aws ssm put-parameter --name /demo/app/db-password --value FakePassw0rd --type SecureString
  3. Read it back: aws ssm get-parameter --name /demo/app/db-password --with-decryption
  4. List by path: aws ssm get-parameters-by-path --path /demo/app --with-decryption
  5. Create a secret: aws secretsmanager create-secret --name demo/db-credentials --secret-string '{"username":"admin","password":"FakePassw0rd"}'
  6. Read it: aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id demo/db-credentials
  7. In the console, open the secret and look at the Rotation settings.
  8. Clean up: aws ssm delete-parameter --name /demo/app/db-host, the same for /demo/app/db-password, and aws secretsmanager delete-secret --secret-id demo/db-credentials --force-delete-without-recovery

Common mistakes

  • Hardcoding passwords in code, in environment files or in a repository.
  • Storing a secret as a plain String parameter.
  • Giving a role access to every secret instead of the ones it needs.
  • Printing secret values in logs or in screenshots.
  • Forgetting to delete practice secrets, which keep costing money.

Key takeaways

  • Keep secrets out of code, and fetch them at runtime.
  • Use Secrets Manager when you need rotation, and Parameter Store for settings and simple secrets.
  • Use SecureString for anything sensitive in Parameter Store.
  • Limit access by path or secret name, and clean up after practice.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS KMS and how the encryption keys behind these services work.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Create and Update Records Cheat Sheet: Writing Data Back and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Reading data is half of a flow. The other half is writing it back. Admin II interviews ask how Create Records and Update Records differ, and how to write…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Reading data is half of a flow. The other half is writing it back. Admin II interviews ask how Create Records and Update Records differ, and how to write many records without hitting limits.

Create and Update at a Glance

Element What it does Key point
Create Records Inserts new records Can store the new record Id in a variable
Update Records Changes existing records Find them by conditions, or use a record or collection
Record variable Holds one record's field values Write it with one element
Record collection Holds many records Write them all with one element

Interview Q&A

1. How do you set the fields in Create Records?

You can set fields one by one with values or resources, or use all values from a record variable that you built earlier.

Tip: Required fields and validation rules still apply when the record is created.

2. How do you get the Id of the new record?

Choose to store the Id of the new record in a variable. Then use that Id in later elements, such as linking a child record.

Tip: Create the parent first, then the children.

3. How can Update Records find the records to change?

Two ways: specify conditions and set fields directly, or use the Ids and values from a record variable or collection.

Tip: With conditions you do not need a Get Records first, but check your filter carefully.

4. When do you use a record variable?

When you need to change a record you already hold, such as the one from Get Records. Assign the new field values to the variable, then update with it.

Tip: The values in the variable are what get written, so check what it holds first.

5. How do you create or update many records?

Add each record to a collection variable with an Assignment inside the loop. After the loop, use one Create Records or Update Records on the whole collection.

Tip: Never put Create, Update or Delete inside the loop.

6. What if the save fails?

Add a fault path to the element. Show a clear message or log the error, so the user is not left with a vague failure.

Tip: Validation rules and required fields are the usual cause.

Scenario Question

"After the rep reviews the open Opportunity, create a follow-up Task and note it on the Opportunity."

  1. Create Records for the Task, storing the new Task Id
  2. Assignment: set the Opportunity variable's NextStep to a short note
  3. Update Records using the Opportunity record variable
  4. Add fault paths to both, then show a confirmation screen

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open your Screen Flow from this series and keep the Get Records element for the open Opportunity.
  2. Add Create Records for Task. Set Subject to {!Default_Subject} and ActivityDate to {!DueDate}. Link it with WhatId set to the Opportunity Id.
  3. Choose to store the Id of the new Task in a variable named NewTaskId.
  4. Add an Assignment that sets {!Get_Open_Opportunity.NextStep} to Follow-up task created.
  5. Add Update Records using the Ids and all values from the record variable {!Get_Open_Opportunity}.
  6. Add fault paths to both elements that lead to a screen with {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.
  7. Debug, then open the Opportunity to check the Next Step and the new Task.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Create Records = new records, can store the new Id
  • Update Records = by conditions, or by record or collection
  • Record variable = one record, collection = many
  • Loop = Assignment adds to a collection
  • After the loop = one Create or Update
  • Fault path on every element that saves

Key Takeaways

  • Build records in variables, then write them with one element.
  • Store the Id of a new record when later steps need it.
  • Never run Create, Update or Delete inside a loop.
  • Add a fault path so errors are readable.

Next up: the Delete Records element and the Roll Back Records element: when to use each and how to stay safe.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Do you update by conditions or by record variable? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Systems Manager: Manage Your Instances Without Opening SSH
item.description: Config shows what changed and whether it follows the rules. The next question is how to actually manage the instances without opening SSH to the world…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Config shows what changed and whether it follows the rules. The next question is how to actually manage the instances without opening SSH to the world. That is where AWS Systems Manager comes in.

What it does

  • Systems Manager is a set of tools to view and manage your AWS resources and nodes from one place.
  • A managed node is an instance (or server) that runs the SSM Agent and can reach Systems Manager.
  • You can connect, run commands and patch without opening inbound port 22 and without key pairs.

The tools to know first

Tool What it does Example use
Session Manager Opens a shell from the console or CLI Log in with no SSH and no bastion host
Run Command Runs a command on one or many nodes Run uptime on a group of instances
Patch Manager Scans and installs patches Patch on a schedule
Parameter Store Stores configuration values and secrets Keep a database name or a secure string
Automation Runs runbooks for common tasks Stop an instance, create an AMI

What an instance needs to become a managed node

  • The SSM Agent installed and running (it comes pre-installed on many Amazon-provided AMIs, including Amazon Linux 2023).
  • An instance profile with an IAM role, for example the AWS managed policy AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  • A network path to the Systems Manager endpoints, such as a public route or VPC endpoints.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open IAM, create a role for EC2, and attach AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.
  2. Launch a small Amazon Linux 2023 instance and choose that role as the IAM instance profile.
  3. In the security group, remove all inbound rules. You will not use SSH.
  4. Open Systems Manager, then Fleet Manager or Session Manager, and wait until the instance shows as a managed node.
  5. In Session Manager, choose Start session, pick the instance, and run whoami.
  6. Open Run Command, choose the document AWS-RunShellScript, enter uptime and run it on the instance.
  7. Check from the CLI: aws ssm describe-instance-information
  8. When you finish practising, terminate the instance and delete the role.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to attach the instance profile, so the node never appears.
  • Using an instance with no route to the Systems Manager endpoints.
  • Leaving port 22 open even though Session Manager makes it unnecessary.
  • Giving the instance role more permissions than it needs.
  • Leaving practice instances running.

Key takeaways

  • Systems Manager manages nodes without SSH or key pairs.
  • An instance needs the agent, an instance profile and network access.
  • Session Manager is for access, Run Command for tasks, Patch Manager for updates.
  • Clean up practice instances when you finish.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, and how to keep secrets out of your code.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Get Records Cheat Sheet: Filters, Sort Order and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Almost every flow starts by reading data. The Get Records element is where that happens, and Admin II interviews love to ask how to set it up and what…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Almost every flow starts by reading data. The Get Records element is where that happens, and Admin II interviews love to ask how to set it up and what happens when nothing comes back.

Get Records at a Glance

Setting What it does Key point
Object Which object to query One object per element
Filter conditions Which records to find AND, OR or custom logic
Sort order Which record comes first Pick a field and direction
How many records Only the first, or all matching First record = one record variable; all = a collection
Which fields to store What the flow keeps Choose only the fields you need

Interview Q&A

1. What does Get Records do?

It finds records in your org that match your conditions and stores them in the flow, so later elements can use them.

Tip: One element queries one object.

2. How do you filter the results?

Add filter conditions on fields. Choose All Conditions Are Met (AND), Any Condition Is Met (OR) or Custom Condition Logic.

Tip: Filter as tightly as you can, so you do not read records you do not need.

3. First record or all records?

Choose Only the first record when you expect one result, such as the Account for a recordId. Choose All records when you need a list, which is stored in a collection.

Tip: Add a sort order so "first" is the one you mean, such as the newest.

4. Which fields should you store?

You can store all fields, or choose only the ones you need. Choosing fields is better for performance and keeps the flow lean.

Tip: Fields you do not store are empty later. Store what you will use.

5. What if no record is found?

The result is empty (null). Add a Decision with the condition "Is Null" for that record or collection, and handle the empty case instead of letting the flow fail later.

Tip: Always plan for zero results.

6. Why not put Get Records inside a loop?

Each Get Records is a query, and a flow has limits on queries in one transaction. Query before the loop, and loop over the collection.

Tip: Same idea for Create, Update and Delete: do them after the loop.

Scenario Question

"A rep opens an Account and the flow must show the most recent open Opportunity."

  1. Add Get Records on Opportunity
  2. Filter: AccountId equals {!recordId} AND IsClosed equals False
  3. Sort by CloseDate, then store only the first record
  4. Add a Decision to check if the result is null, then show a screen with the Opportunity name and amount

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open your Screen Flow from this series in Flow Builder.
  2. Add a Get Records element, label it Get Open Opportunity, object Opportunity.
  3. Set conditions with All Conditions Are Met (AND): AccountId equals {!recordId} and IsClosed equals False.
  4. Sort by CloseDate ascending and choose Only the first record. Store only the fields Name and Amount.
  5. Add a Decision named Found? with the outcome Is Null for {!Get_Open_Opportunity} set to True, and a default outcome for found.
  6. Add one screen for each path, showing {!Get_Open_Opportunity.Name} on the found path and a short message on the empty path.
  7. Debug the flow with an Account that has an open Opportunity, then with one that does not.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • One object per Get Records element
  • Filters: AND, OR or custom logic
  • Sort so the first record is the one you want
  • First record = record variable, all records = collection
  • Store only the fields you need
  • No result = null, so check with a Decision
  • Never inside a loop

Key Takeaways

  • Get Records reads data into the flow, so set it up carefully.
  • Tight filters and chosen fields keep flows fast.
  • Always handle the case where nothing is found.
  • Query before a loop, not inside it.

Next up: the Create Records and Update Records elements: record variables, collections and what each one writes.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. How do you handle the "no records found" case? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Config: Track Resource Changes and Check Compliance
item.description: CloudTrail tells me who made a change. The next question is different: what did the resource look like before, and does it follow my rules? That is the job…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
CloudTrail tells me who made a change. The next question is different: what did the resource look like before, and does it follow my rules? That is the job of AWS Config.

What AWS Config does

  • It records the configuration of supported AWS resources and keeps a history of how each one changed.
  • It checks those configurations against rules and reports each resource as compliant or non-compliant.
  • It works per Region, so you set it up in each Region you use.

CloudTrail and Config together

Question Service
Who made this API call, and when? CloudTrail
What did this resource look like last week? Config
Is this resource following our rule? Config

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Configuration recorder Records resource settings Choose all resources or specific types
Configuration item A snapshot of one resource at a point in time Builds the resource timeline
Config rule A check on a resource setting AWS managed rules or your own
Compliance status Result of a rule COMPLIANT or NON_COMPLIANT
Remediation An action to fix a non-compliant resource Can run an SSM Automation document

Examples of managed rules

  • s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited flags buckets that allow public reads.
  • restricted-ssh flags security groups that allow SSH from anywhere.
  • encrypted-volumes flags EBS volumes that are not encrypted.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open AWS Config and choose Set up (or Get started).
  2. Record specific resource types such as S3 buckets and security groups, to keep it small.
  3. Let it create an S3 bucket for the delivery channel and the service-linked role.
  4. Add the managed rule s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited, then add restricted-ssh.
  5. Wait for the first evaluation, then open Rules and read the compliance status.
  6. Open Resources, pick a security group and read its resource timeline.
  7. Check from the CLI: aws configservice describe-compliance-by-config-rule
  8. When you finish practising, stop the recorder: aws configservice stop-configuration-recorder --configuration-recorder-name default

Common mistakes

  • Setting up Config in one Region and expecting it everywhere.
  • Recording every resource type for a small practice account without checking the cost.
  • Adding rules but never looking at the non-compliant list.
  • Forgetting to stop the recorder after practice.

Key takeaways

  • Config records how resources change and checks them against rules.
  • CloudTrail answers who, Config answers what and whether it is compliant.
  • Start with a few managed rules and review the results.
  • Watch the cost, because it depends on what you record and evaluate.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS Systems Manager and how it manages instances without opening SSH.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Resources Cheat Sheet: Variables, Constants, Formulas and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Every flow needs places to keep and calculate values. Admin II interviews ask which resource to use and why: a variable, a constant, a formula or a text…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Every flow needs places to keep and calculate values. Admin II interviews ask which resource to use and why: a variable, a constant, a formula or a text template.

The Four Resources at a Glance

Resource What it holds Key point
Variable A value that can change while the flow runs Single value, record or collection
Constant A fixed value Cannot be changed by the flow
Formula A calculated value Read-only, recalculated each time you use it
Text template Formatted text with merge fields Good for messages and email bodies

Interview Q&A

1. What is a variable?

A named container for a value. Choose its data type (Text, Number, Currency, Boolean, Date, Date/Time or Record) and whether it holds one value or a collection.

Tip: Name it for what it holds, such as TasksToUpdate.

2. What do "Available for input" and "Available for output" mean?

Input lets a value be passed into the flow, for example recordId from a record page. Output lets a value be passed out to a parent flow or another caller.

Tip: Tick only what you need.

3. When do you use a constant?

When a value never changes during the flow, such as a default Task subject. Change it in one place instead of searching every element.

Tip: A constant cannot be updated by an Assignment.

4. What is a formula resource?

A value calculated from other values, such as a due date of today plus 7 days. It is read-only and works out the answer each time the flow uses it.

Tip: Pick the formula's data type to match where you will use it.

5. When do you use a text template?

When you need a longer message that mixes text and merge fields, such as a confirmation screen or an email body.

Tip: Use rich text for formatting, plain text for simple messages.

6. How do you refer to a resource?

Wrap its name in curly brackets with an exclamation mark, such as {!recordId}. Global values work the same way, for example {!$Flow.CurrentDate} and {!$User.Id}.

Tip: The resource picker avoids typing mistakes.

Scenario Question

"Create a follow-up Task due 7 days from today, with the same subject every time."

  1. Create a constant Default_Subject with the value Follow up call
  2. Create a formula DueDate of type Date: {!$Flow.CurrentDate} + 7
  3. Use both in the Create Records element for the Task
  4. Show a text template on the confirmation screen

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open your Screen Flow from this series in Flow Builder.
  2. Choose New Resource, then Constant. Name it Default_Subject, type Text, value Follow up call.
  3. Add a Formula named DueDate, data type Date, with {!$Flow.CurrentDate} + 7.
  4. In the Create Records element for the Task, set Subject to {!Default_Subject} and ActivityDate to {!DueDate}.
  5. Add a Text Template named ConfirmMessage: Follow-up created for {!DueDate}.
  6. Show {!ConfirmMessage} on the last screen, then Debug and check the Task.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Changes at runtime = Variable
  • Never changes = Constant
  • Calculated, read-only = Formula
  • Message with merge fields = Text template
  • Today's date = {!$Flow.CurrentDate}
  • Refer to anything = {!Name}

Key Takeaways

  • Use a variable when the value changes, a constant when it does not.
  • A formula calculates and cannot be assigned to.
  • A text template builds readable messages.
  • Clear names make flows easy to maintain.

Next up: the Get Records element: filters, sort order and how many records to store.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which resource do you forget to use? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS CloudTrail: See Who Did What in Your AWS Account
item.description: Last time I set up an alarm to be told when something goes wrong. The next question is different: who did what in my account? When a setting changes or a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Last time I set up an alarm to be told when something goes wrong. The next question is different: who did what in my account? When a setting changes or a resource disappears, the answer comes from AWS CloudTrail.

What CloudTrail does

  • It records API activity in your account: who made the call, what they did, when, and from where.
  • That includes actions in the console, the CLI, SDKs and other AWS services.
  • It is the first place to look after a surprise change or a security question.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Event One recorded API call Shows user, action, time, source IP
Event history A searchable view of recent events Management events, last 90 days, per Region
Trail A setting that delivers events to an S3 bucket Keeps history longer than 90 days
Management events Actions on resources Examples: CreateTopic, RunInstances, DeleteBucket
Data events Actions on the data inside resources Examples: S3 object reads, Lambda invokes. Off by default

Event history or a trail?

  • Event history is on by default, needs no setup and covers the last 90 days of management events.
  • A trail stores events in S3 so you can keep them, search them later and share them across the organization.
  • A trail can apply to all Regions, so activity in a Region you never use still gets recorded.

Hands-on: find who did something

  1. Open CloudTrail, then Event history.
  2. Filter by Event name and search for CreateTopic. That is the SNS topic from my last post.
  3. Open the event and read the user name, event time and source IP address.
  4. Create a trail: choose Create trail, name it management-events, let it create a new S3 bucket, and keep Management events selected.
  5. Turn on Apply trail to all Regions.
  6. Check it from the CLI: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=CreateTopic --max-results 5

Common mistakes

  • Treating Event history as permanent when it only keeps 90 days.
  • Creating a trail for one Region only.
  • Turning on data events everywhere without thinking about cost.
  • Leaving the log bucket open to more people than needed.

Key takeaways

  • CloudTrail answers who did what, when and from where.
  • Event history is free and quick, a trail keeps the history.
  • Use a trail that covers all Regions.
  • Protect the bucket that holds the logs.

Tomorrow I'll look at AWS Config, which tracks how your resources looked over time.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Decisions and Loops Cheat Sheet: Branching, Looping and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Almost every real flow is built from two elements: a Decision that chooses a path and a Loop that works through a list. Admin II interviews love them…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Almost every real flow is built from two elements: a Decision that chooses a path and a Loop that works through a list. Admin II interviews love them, especially the rule about what never goes inside a loop.

The Two Elements at a Glance

Element What it does Key point
Decision Sends the flow down one path Outcomes are checked in order, first match wins
Default outcome The path when no outcome matches Always plan for it
Loop Goes through a collection one item at a time Has a For Each path and an After Last Item path
Assignment Changes variable values Use it inside the loop to build a collection

Interview Q&A

1. How does a Decision pick a path?

It checks its outcomes from top to bottom and takes the first one whose conditions are met. If none match, the Default outcome runs.

Tip: Put the most specific outcome first.

2. Can an outcome have several conditions?

Yes. Combine them with AND, OR or a custom logic such as 1 AND (2 OR 3).

Tip: Name outcomes clearly, for example "Has open tasks".

3. What does a Loop need?

A collection variable to loop over. The loop gives you one record at a time as the current item.

Tip: Name the loop after what it holds, such as Loop_Tasks.

4. What are the two paths out of a Loop?

For Each Item runs once per record. After Last Item runs once when the loop is done.

Tip: Do the saving after the last item, not during the loop.

5. What should you never put inside a loop?

Create, Update, Delete or Get Records elements. They run once per item and can hit governor limits.

Tip: Collect changes in a collection, then save once after the loop.

6. How do you change records in a loop the right way?

Use an Assignment to set the field on the current item, then add the item to a second collection. After the loop, run one Update Records on that collection.

Tip: Check the collection is not empty before the update.

Scenario Question

"Close all open Tasks on an Account when the rep clicks a button."

  1. Get Records for open Tasks on the Account, storing all records
  2. A Decision checks that at least one Task was found
  3. A Loop goes through the Tasks, with an Assignment that sets Status to Completed and adds the Task to a collection
  4. After the last item, one Update Records saves the collection

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow with a Text variable recordId, available for input.
  2. Add Get Records on Task where WhatId equals {!recordId} and IsClosed is False. Store all records.
  3. Add a Decision with an outcome "Found tasks" where the Get Records result Is Null equals False.
  4. Create a record collection variable TasksToUpdate for Task.
  5. Add a Loop over the Get Records result. Inside it, add an Assignment that sets {!Loop_Tasks.Status} to Completed, then adds {!Loop_Tasks} to {!TasksToUpdate}.
  6. After the last item, add Update Records using {!TasksToUpdate}, and a closing screen.
  7. Run Debug on an Account with open Tasks and check the Tasks are completed.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Pick a path = Decision
  • Order = Top to bottom, first match
  • No match = Default outcome
  • One at a time = Loop
  • Save once = After Last Item
  • Never in a loop = Records elements

Key Takeaways

  • A Decision takes the first matching outcome.
  • A Loop works on one record at a time.
  • Collect changes in a collection inside the loop.
  • Save once after the last item.

Next up: Flow resources: variables, constants and formulas.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which do you use more, Decisions or Loops? Tell me below.

item.title: I built a GitOps pipeline from scratch (Jenkins, ArgoCD, Terraform, EKS), and what broke
item.description: I wanted one project where a git push ends up as a running pod with no manual steps, then the same thing on real AWS. Here is what I built and what went…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
I wanted one project where a git push ends up as a running pod with no manual steps, then the same thing on real AWS. Here is what I built and what went wrong.

The flow

  1. I push a change to GitHub.
  2. Jenkins notices it by polling (every 2 minutes), builds a Docker image and pushes it to Docker Hub.
  3. Jenkins commits the new image tag into k8s/deployment.yaml.
  4. ArgoCD sees the manifest change and syncs it to Kubernetes.

I proved it by changing the page heading and watching the new text appear without touching anything after the push. Repo: https://github.com/RobinSishodia/aws-eks-gitops-argocd

Terraform and EKS

I rebuilt the cluster on AWS with Terraform: a VPC with public and private subnets and a NAT gateway, plus an EKS cluster with a managed node group. ArgoCD ran on it with the app Synced and Healthy. Then I destroyed all 56 resources, verified nothing was left, and deleted the access key.

What went wrong

  1. Jenkins rebuilt its own commits. The pipeline pushes a commit, so auto-triggering would loop forever. I added a guard that skips any build whose latest commit says [skip ci]. Jenkins core does not honour that tag by itself. I also once put that exact text in my own commit message and skipped a build I wanted.
  2. AWS Free plan instance types. t3.medium was rejected as not free-tier eligible. I queried the eligible types and switched to c7i-flex.large.
  3. Nodes that never joined. The EKS Terraform module does not install vpc-cni, kube-proxy or CoreDNS by default, so the nodes had no networking and the node group hung for hours. Declaring the add-ons fixed it. I also added a 25-minute create timeout so a stuck build fails fast.

What I would do next

A real GitHub webhook instead of polling (it needs Jenkins reachable from the internet), then monitoring with Prometheus and Grafana.

item.title: AWS CloudWatch Alarms and SNS: Get Notified When Something Goes Wrong
item.description: In the last two posts I set up several accounts and a way for people to sign in. Now the question every real environment hits: when something goes wrong…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
In the last two posts I set up several accounts and a way for people to sign in. Now the question every real environment hits: when something goes wrong, who finds out, and how fast? The basic answer on AWS is a CloudWatch alarm that sends a message through Amazon SNS.

What each service does

  • Amazon CloudWatch collects metrics, such as CPU use or estimated charges, and can watch them with alarms.
  • CloudWatch alarm compares a metric to a threshold and moves between three states: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA.
  • Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) sends a message to everyone subscribed to a topic, by email, SMS or other targets.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Metric A number measured over time Example: CPUUtilization or EstimatedCharges
Alarm A rule on one metric Threshold, period and number of periods
SNS topic A channel for messages Alarms publish to it
Subscription Who receives the topic An email subscription must be confirmed
Alarm action What the alarm does on a state change Often: publish to an SNS topic

Why a topic and not a direct email

  • One topic can notify a whole team, and you can add people without touching the alarm.
  • The same topic can be reused by many alarms.
  • Later you can add other targets, such as a chat tool or a Lambda function.

Hands-on: a billing alert in your own account

  1. Sign in with a user that can open the Billing console, and turn on Receive CloudWatch billing alerts in Billing preferences.
  2. Switch the Region to US East (N. Virginia), because billing metrics are only published there.
  3. Open SNS, create a Standard topic named billing-alerts, and add an Email subscription with your address.
  4. Open the email and choose Confirm subscription. Until you do, nothing is delivered.
  5. Open CloudWatch, then Alarms, then Create alarm. Select the metric Billing > Total Estimated Charge and set a threshold such as 5 USD.
  6. For the alarm action choose In alarm, send to the billing-alerts topic, and create the alarm.
  7. Test the notification path with the CLI: aws cloudwatch set-alarm-state --alarm-name <your-alarm> --state-value ALARM --state-reason "test" and check that the email arrives.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to confirm the email subscription.
  • Creating the billing alarm in a Region other than US East (N. Virginia).
  • Setting the threshold so high that the alarm never fires.
  • Sending alerts to one personal inbox that nobody else watches.

Key takeaways

  • An alarm watches a metric, SNS delivers the message.
  • Use a topic so you can add people and targets later.
  • Confirm subscriptions and test the path on purpose.
  • Start with a billing alarm in every new account.

Tomorrow I'll look at how to see who did what in your account, with AWS CloudTrail.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Fault Paths Cheat Sheet: Handling Errors in Screen Flows and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Things go wrong, even in a good Screen Flow: a required field is empty, a record is locked, a validation rule fires. Admin II interviews ask how you handle…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Things go wrong, even in a good Screen Flow: a required field is empty, a record is locked, a validation rule fires. Admin II interviews ask how you handle it so the user sees a clear message instead of a scary error.

What Happens Without a Fault Path

If an element fails and you did nothing about it, the user sees a generic unhandled fault error and Salesforce emails the details to the admin. A fault path lets you decide what happens instead.

Idea What it means Key point
Fault connector A second path out of an element that can fail Drawn as a red dashed line
Fault message The text of the error {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
Fault screen A screen that explains the problem Shown instead of the crash
Debug Run the flow with test data Use it to trigger a failure on purpose

Interview Q&A

1. What is a fault path?

It is the path a flow takes when an element fails. You add it from the element with the Fault connector.

Tip: Think of it as the "if this fails" branch.

2. Which elements can have one?

Elements that can fail, such as Create, Update, Get and Delete Records, actions and subflows. Screen elements do not get one.

Tip: Put it on every element that changes data.

3. How do you show the error to the user?

Send the fault connector to a Screen and add a Display Text component with {!$Flow.FaultMessage}.

Tip: Add a friendly sentence above it, such as "We could not save your call."

4. Should users see the raw message?

Usually not. Raw messages can be technical. Show a plain message to the user and keep the detail for the admin.

Tip: Say what to do next, for example "Contact your admin."

5. How does the admin find out?

Salesforce sends a flow error email for unhandled faults. In your own fault path you can also send an email or create a record that logs the error.

Tip: A log record is easier to search than a pile of emails.

6. How do you test it?

Use Debug and cause a failure on purpose, such as leaving a required field empty, then check that the fault screen appears.

Tip: A fault path you never tested is a guess.

Scenario Question

"The call log flow sometimes fails and reps just see an error."

  1. Open the Screen Flow and find the Create Records element for the Task
  2. Add a Fault connector from it to a new screen
  3. Show a friendly message plus {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  4. Debug with a failing case, then activate the new version

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open yesterday's Screen Flow in Flow Builder.
  2. On the Create Records element that creates the Task, choose Add Fault Path.
  3. Add a Screen after it named Something went wrong.
  4. In that screen add Display Text: We could not save your call. Details: {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  5. Run Debug and leave the Task Subject empty so the create fails.
  6. Check that the fault screen appears, then Save and Activate the new version.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Second path out = Fault connector
  • Error text = {!$Flow.FaultMessage}
  • Show it = Fault screen
  • Screens = no fault path
  • Test it = Debug a failure
  • Unhandled = Error email to admin

Key Takeaways

  • Add a fault path to every element that changes data.
  • Show a friendly message, not a crash.
  • Keep the technical detail for the admin.
  • Test the failure on purpose.

Next up: Flow decisions and loops, the two elements behind most real flows.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. How do your flows handle errors? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS IAM Identity Center: Single Sign-On Across Your AWS Accounts
item.description: Yesterday I set up an organization with several accounts. Now the next question: how do people get into those accounts without a pile of IAM users and…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Yesterday I set up an organization with several accounts. Now the next question: how do people get into those accounts without a pile of IAM users and long-term access keys? The answer is AWS IAM Identity Center.

What it does

  • It is the AWS service for workforce single sign-on across the accounts in your organization and supported applications.
  • People sign in once at the AWS access portal and pick the account and role they need.
  • Access is given through temporary credentials, so there are no long-term keys to lose.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Identity source Where users and groups live Built-in directory, Active Directory or an external identity provider
Permission set A template of permissions Identity Center creates a role from it in each assigned account
Assignment Links a user or group to an account with a permission set Assign groups, not single users
Access portal The sign-in page for your users One URL for all accounts

How it fits with Organizations

  • Enable it in the management account with AWS Organizations turned on.
  • Choose the home Region carefully, because it is hard to change later.
  • Roles created from permission sets show up in each account with names starting AWSReservedSSO_.
  • Session length is set per permission set.

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open IAM Identity Center in the management account and choose Enable.
  2. Under Groups, create a group named ReadOnly, then create a user and add them to it.
  3. Under Permission sets, create one that uses the AWS managed ViewOnlyAccess or ReadOnlyAccess policy.
  4. Under AWS accounts, select an account, choose Assign users or groups, and pick the group and the permission set.
  5. Open the access portal URL, sign in as the user, and choose the account and role.
  6. Optional: run aws configure sso, then aws sso login, and check with aws sts get-caller-identity.

Common mistakes

  • Creating IAM users for every person instead of using Identity Center.
  • Assigning permission sets to single users, which gets hard to manage.
  • Giving broad access when a read-only permission set is enough.
  • Forgetting MFA for the people who sign in.

Key takeaways

  • Use Identity Center for people and IAM roles for workloads.
  • Define access once in a permission set and assign it to groups.
  • Prefer temporary credentials over long-term keys.
  • Keep MFA on for every user.

Tomorrow I'll look at what happens when something goes wrong in your accounts, starting with how to be notified.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Screen Flow Launch Cheat Sheet: Quick Actions, Lightning Pages and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: A Screen Flow only helps if users can find it. Admin II interviews ask where you would launch one, how it knows which record it is on, and who is allowed…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A Screen Flow only helps if users can find it. Admin II interviews ask where you would launch one, how it knows which record it is on, and who is allowed to run it.

The 4 Ways to Launch a Screen Flow

Where How Key point
Quick action Action of type Flow on an object Shows as a button on the record page
Lightning page The Flow component Runs inline on the page
URL or button /flow/FlowApiName Good for links and custom buttons
Utility bar Flow utility item Always available in the app

Interview Q&A

1. Why must the flow be active?

Users can only run an active flow. Activate it before you add it to a page, an action or a link.

Tip: Test with Debug first, then activate.

2. How do you add a quick action?

In Object Manager, create an action of type Flow, pick the flow and give it a short label. Then add it to the page layout so the button appears.

Tip: Keep the label short so it fits on the button.

3. How do you embed the flow on a page?

In the Lightning App Builder, drag the Flow component onto the page and choose the flow.

Tip: One flow per section keeps the page clean.

4. How does the flow get the current record?

Create a Text variable named recordId and tick Available for input. Salesforce passes the record Id in when the flow runs from a record page.

Tip: The variable name must match exactly.

5. Who can run it?

Users need access to the flow, for example the Run Flows permission, or access given through a profile or permission set.

Tip: Test as a real user, not only as an admin.

6. What happens when the flow finishes?

Show a confirmation screen, or use the flow's finish setting to restart it or send the user elsewhere.

Tip: End with a clear message so the user knows it worked.

Scenario Question

"Let reps log a call from the Account page."

  1. Build the Screen Flow with a recordId variable
  2. Activate it
  3. Create a Flow quick action on Account
  4. Add it to the page layout and test as a rep

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Open yesterday's Screen Flow and add a Text variable recordId, available for input.
  2. Use {!recordId} as the WhatId when it creates the Task.
  3. Save and Activate the flow.
  4. In Object Manager, create a Flow quick action on Account and add it to the page layout.
  5. Open an Account, run the action, and check that the Task is linked to that Account.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Run from a record = Quick action
  • Embed inline = Flow component
  • Link to it = /flow/ApiName
  • Know the record = recordId
  • Must be = Active
  • Access = Run Flows

Key Takeaways

  • Activate before you place it.
  • Use recordId for record context.
  • Pick the launch spot that suits the user.
  • Test as a real user.

Next up: Flow error handling and fault paths in Screen Flows.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Where do your users launch Screen Flows? Tell me below.

item.title: AWS Organizations: Multiple Accounts, OUs and Service Control Policies
item.description: So far I have secured root, set a budget, turned on CloudTrail and CloudWatch, and added tags. All of that sits in one account. The next step is the…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
So far I have secured root, set a budget, turned on CloudTrail and CloudWatch, and added tags. All of that sits in one account. The next step is the structure around it: AWS Organizations.

Why more than one account

  • An AWS account is a strong boundary for security, cost and blast radius.
  • A mistake in a sandbox account cannot touch production.
  • Each account has its own root user, IAM and limits, so teams can work separately.

The building blocks

Term What it is Notes
Organization The group of accounts you manage together Created from one account
Management account The account that creates the organization and pays the bill SCPs do not apply to it
Member accounts Every other account in the organization One per workload or team
OU An organizational unit that groups accounts Policies on an OU apply to its accounts
SCP A service control policy Sets the maximum permissions, never grants them

Consolidated billing

  • All member accounts roll up to one bill on the management account.
  • Usage across accounts can count together for volume discounts.
  • Tags still let you split cost by project or owner.

How SCPs behave

  • An SCP is a guardrail: an action must be allowed by the SCP and by the identity's own IAM policy.
  • They apply to IAM users and roles in member accounts, including the account root user.
  • They do not apply to the management account, so keep workloads out of it.
  • Use all features mode to turn SCPs on.

A simple starting structure

  • Security OU: logging and audit accounts
  • Workloads OU: production and non-production accounts
  • Sandbox OU: learning and experiments, with tighter SCPs

Hands-on: try it in your own account

  1. Open AWS Organizations and choose Create an organization.
  2. Check that MFA is on for the management account root user.
  3. Create an OU named Sandbox.
  4. Choose Add an AWS account, then Create an AWS account, and give it a unique email address and a name. Move it into the Sandbox OU.
  5. Open Policies, enable service control policies, and attach a deny policy to the Sandbox OU, for example one that stops the account leaving the organization.
  6. Sign in to the management account and assume the OrganizationAccountAccessRole in the new account to check it works.

Common mistakes

  • Running workloads in the management account.
  • Using SCPs as if they grant permissions. They only limit.
  • Reusing one email address for several accounts. Each account needs a unique one.
  • Attaching SCPs to the organization root before testing on a Sandbox OU.

Key takeaways

  • Use separate accounts as security and cost boundaries.
  • Group accounts into OUs and attach policy once.
  • SCPs set the maximum, IAM still grants.
  • Keep the management account for administration only.

Tomorrow I'll look at how people and tools sign in across these accounts.

Part of #120DaysOfAWS.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Screens Cheat Sheet: User Input, Validation and Admin II Interview Q&A
item.description: Screens are how a Flow talks to the user. Admin II interviews ask about them because input, validation and navigation decide whether a Screen Flow is easy…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Screens are how a Flow talks to the user. Admin II interviews ask about them because input, validation and navigation decide whether a Screen Flow is easy to use and safe to trust.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it does Key point
Input components Collect text, numbers, dates and more The value is stored for later elements
Choice components Radio buttons, picklists, checkboxes Fed by a choice or a choice set
Display components Show text, sections and messages Guide the user
Validation Required, or a formula with an error message Stops bad data early

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Screen element?

The element that shows a user interface and collects input. Screens only work in Screen Flows, not in record-triggered or autolaunched flows.

Tip: Use a Screen whenever a person has to type or choose something.

2. How do you use what the user entered?

Each screen component keeps its value. Reference it with the component's API name, for example {!Subject.value}, in later elements such as Create Records.

Tip: Give components clear API names. You will type them a lot.

3. How do you validate input?

Mark a field Required, or open its Validate Input setting and add a formula with an error message. The user cannot continue until the formula is true.

Tip: Stop bad data at the screen, not after it is saved.

4. Can you hide components?

Yes. Set Component Visibility conditions on a field or a section, so it only appears when an earlier answer calls for it.

Tip: Show only what the user needs for this case.

5. Where do choices come from?

Create a Choice resource for a fixed option, or a Record Choice Set or Picklist Choice Set to load options from records or from a field's picklist values.

Tip: Build a choice set once and reuse it across screens.

6. How does the user move through the flow?

With the Next, Previous and Finish buttons. You choose which of them each screen shows, and whether the user can go back.

Tip: Check the Back button on every screen. Going back can change data you already saved.

Scenario Question

"Let sales reps log a call from a Screen Flow."

  1. Screen: Subject (text), Priority (picklist), Due Date (date)
  2. Create Records: a Task, with fields from the screen inputs
  3. Confirmation screen that shows the new Task Id
  4. Fault path on Create Records, then Debug

Hands-On: Try It in Your Own Org

  1. Create a Screen Flow and add a Screen with a Text input named Subject.
  2. Add a Picklist choice for Priority and a Date input for Due Date.
  3. Make Subject Required, and add a Validate formula so the date cannot be in the past.
  4. Add Create Records for Task and map the three inputs.
  5. Add a confirmation screen, run Debug, then add the flow to a Lightning page.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Show UI = Screen
  • Read input = {!Name.value}
  • Block bad data = Validate Input
  • Hide fields = Component Visibility
  • Pick from a list = Choice or choice set
  • Save the data = Create Records after the screen

Key Takeaways

  • Screens belong to Screen Flows.
  • Validate on the screen.
  • Reuse choice sets.
  • Save once, after the user is done.

Next up: running a Screen Flow from buttons, Lightning pages and quick actions.

Part of #120DaysOfSalesforce. Which Screen component do you use most? Tell me below.

item.title: I built a tiny GitHub repo auditor, and it found my own mess
item.description: Just shipped repo-health-report: a tiny, dependency-free Python tool that audits your GitHub repos through the REST API. It flags missing licenses…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Just shipped repo-health-report: a tiny, dependency-free Python tool that audits your GitHub repos through the REST API.

It flags missing licenses, descriptions, topics and READMEs, plus pull requests that have gone stale. It also runs as a scheduled GitHub Action and writes the results to the job summary.

On my own account it found 15 repos without a license. I fixed 12 of them in an afternoon.

What it checks

  • Missing license
  • Missing description or topics
  • Missing README
  • Open pull requests with no activity for 30+ days

Try it

python repo_health_report.py <github-username>

Code and setup: https://github.com/RobinSishodia/repo-health-report

Feedback and issues welcome. If it's useful to you, a star helps.
